Lord Krishna said: There is no destruction, O Arjuna, for a yogi either here or hereafter. A transcendentalist is never put to grief, My dear friend. (6.40)

The less evolved unsuccessful yogi is reborn in the house of the pious and prosperous after attaining heaven and living there for many years. The highly evolved unsuccessful yogi does not go to heaven, but is born in a spiritually advanced family. A birth like this is very difficult, indeed, to obtain in this world. (6.41-42)

There he or she regains the knowledge acquired in the previous life, and strives again to achieve perfection, O Arjuna. (6.43)

**The unsuccessful yogi is instinctively carried towards God by virtue of the impressions of yogic practices of previous lives. Even the inquirer of yoga — the union with God — surpasses those who perform Vedic rituals. (6.44)**

The yogi, who diligently strives, becomes completely free from all imperfections after gradually perfecting through many incarnations, and reaches the Supreme Abode. (6.45)

->**WHO IS THE BEST YOGI**<-

The yogi, who is devoted to meditation, is superior to the ascetics. The yogi is superior to the Vedic scholars. The yogi is superior to the ritualists. Therefore, O Arjuna, be a yogi. (6.46)

**And I consider the yogi-devotee — who lovingly contemplates on Me with supreme faith, and whose mind is ever absorbed in Me — to be the best of all the yogis. (See also 12.02 and 18.66) (6.47)**

# BOOK IV.

The mind of the ascetic, which was inclined towards ignorance and directed outwards—bowed down towards objects, and having the experience of objects as its fruit—is now turned towards discrimination. That is, it enters the right path and is directed inwards toward "Isolation"—it has Isolation as its result, or is possessed of the germ of Isolation.*

Now, by describing the causes of the impediments that occur to the mind flowing in the path of discrimination, he mentions the means of abandoning those obstacles:—†

->तच्छिद्रेषु प्रत्ययान्तराणि संस्कारेभ्यः ॥ २६ ॥<-

*Aph. 26.* In the intervals thereof, other thoughts arise from the self-continuant impressions.

Different thoughts, characterized by "non-abstraction," which arise in the intervals or gaps in the mind of the ascetic abiding in meditation, spring up in the shape of "I," "mine," etc., from the former impressions of the mind produced by the perceptions of non-abstraction, even though these are now weakened.‡

Therefore, such thoughts must be abandoned by extirpating their causes. This is what is to be stated.

He now states that the methods of abandoning these are as they have been described before:§

->हानं तेषां क्लेशवदुक्तम् ॥ २७ ॥<-

*Aph. 27.* The means of the avoidance of these are explained to be as in the case of the afflictions.

<margin>* The mind that was previously leaning toward ignorance, outward-facing, and bearing the fruit of object-enjoyment, is now leaning toward discrimination and the path of truth, bearing the fruit of Isolation or starting the process of Isolation.</margin>
<margin>† He mentions the way to renounce these by explaining their causes in the mind that is flowing toward discrimination.</margin>
<margin>‡ In the intervals of the ascetic's meditation, thoughts of distraction arise from previous impressions of worldly experience, even if those impressions are waning. The meaning is that one must destroy them by cutting off the root of the internal organs.</margin>
<margin>§ He states that the means of removal has been described previously.</margin>

<summary>The author explains that even in meditation, past impressions can create distractions, and these must be cleared using the same techniques previously applied to the "afflictions" (Kleshas).</summary>

<header>Impedimentum.i.</header>

Impediment i. The first part commonly concerns the obstacles to marriage. The first is about the impediment in general; the second, error of the person; the third, the impediment of condition; the fourth, the impediment of the vow; the fifth, the impediment of carnal kinship; the sixth, the impediment of spiritual kinship, that is to say, of godparenthood; the seventh, legal kinship, that is to say, adoption; the eighth, the impediment of sin; the ninth, of <term>diffulto</term> <gloss>difficulty</gloss>, that is, of disparate faith, and this is the tenth; the eleventh, of force or fear; the twelfth, of the impediment of holy orders; the thirteenth, of the bond to another woman; the fourteenth, of the justice of public honesty; the fifteenth, of affinity; the sixteenth, of the inability to unite; the seventeenth, of marriage made against the interdict of the church; the eighteenth, of the impediment of times and seasons. And of these said impediments, there are verses in which they are explained according to the said order, thus: Error, condition, vow, kinship, crime, disparity of cult, force, order, bond, honesty; if you are akin, if by chance you cannot copulate, these things known forbid marriages, it retracts the joined, the prohibition of the church, and also the forbidden times, they impede it from being made, they allow what is done to be held.

¶ Chapter 2. What things impede a marriage already made. It is answered: there are 12 which not only impede a marriage from being made, but even undo the one that is already made. Which things are placed in the first three verses in the nearby text. ¶ And they understand that they undo the marriage already made if they passed before the marriage, but if they supervened after the marriage was already rightly made, such as sister-in-law status or sin, they do not undo it. ¶ Even if it is not followed by carnal union. <note>see Summa Confessorum, book 4, title 30, question 1, B.</note> Saved for one case, this by the vow of religion with effect, when someone, having made the marriage, before the carnal union entered into religion. <note>see Extra, "On the conversion of married persons," chapter "Venit," c. "ex parte n." z. H.</note> There it is said clearly that a marriage contracted legitimately by words of the present can in no case be undone, even if one of the contractors were made a heretic, because while the other lives they pass to second vows, unless one enters into religion. <note>B. Of betrothals, "commissum." But it must be waited for until the profession is made, as Thomas puts it in the 4th, distinction 27.</note> He means until the religion in general is at least tacitly obligated, because if he did not want to change his life absolutely, the benefit of the one who enters is not to be given to another without his consent. <note>see in the chapter "beneficium," of rules, book 6, B. For at least it is not undone, nor even according to Pe. Similarly to this, see below "votum," 4, f. G., at the end.</note> And this is to be guarded the same for the reception of holy orders, for the marriage is as well undone as some wished to say, but the contrary is declared in an Extravagante of John XXII that begins "Antiqua."

<column-break/>

¶ Chapter 3. What things are those that impede a marriage that is to be made, but do not impede or undo the one that is already made. It is answered: the first are the two things mentioned above in the 1st section, that is to say, the development of the church, nor the time of the fairs, of which it will be said below in Impediment 16 and Impediment 17. Also there are some sins of which see below Impediment 8, section 1. Item, it impedes betrothals that were first begun with another; see it below under "sponsalia," section 8. Item, it impedes the catechism that is done before baptism; see it below Impediment 6, section z. Item, it impedes the simple vow; see it below Impediment 4, section i. n. z.

¶ Chapter 4. If any custom impedes a marriage that is to be made or undoes the one that is already made. It is answered according to Hostiensis: if the custom is approved by the Pope that the marriage is not to be made, or if it is already made that it be undone, certainly it will impede and undo in any cases that the canonical constitution can do this. <note>Extra, "On spiritual kinship," chapter 1, n. c. ff. c. Extra, "On consanguinity," n. thus.</note> That the choice of the Pope has the force of law. But if the custom is not approved by the Pope nor disapproved, then to avoid the scandal that could happen by acting against it, the marriage that is to be made they will impede; the one that is already made is not undone. This same thing says Bernard in his "Novella." A. The same in the "Summa Confessorum," title, question 2.

¶ Chapter 5. What is to be held or done when the doctors disagree concerning the impediments of marriage. It is answered according to Hostiensis: wherever the doctors say by their glosses that the marriage is undone, if they do not bring forward an express contrary law, you must adhere to those who say the contrary. <note>Extra, "On witnesses," l. 3, "ex quodam" at the end. A. The same in the "Summa Confessorum," same title, question 3.</note>
